name: Ketovore

angle.text: Ketovore is followed by people who want keto-style fat loss with the simplicity of a meat-centred plate, aiming for a leaner body and less bloat. The hybrid label has no trials of its own; evidence comes from keto and low-carb diet research generally.

summary: Keto with a meat-first bias and a few plants allowed; a hybrid label with no trials of its own.
note: Neighbouring carnivore diet is described by dietitians as a fad diet with nutrient and lipid concerns.
currentQuick:
Ketovore blends keto and carnivore: mostly meat and animal fat, very low carbohydrate, with a small selection of plant foods. The name is informal.
No clinical trials have tested it for body composition or appearance. Evidence comes from studies of the broader ketogenic diet.
How it works: Cutting carbohydrate pushes the liver to produce ketone bodies as an alternative fuel, which is the basis of the ketogenic diet. Followers say adding a few plants offers variety and fibre while keeping the meat focus.
Risks and caveats: Ketogenic diets can cause constipation, raised blood lipids and kidney stones, and medical supervision is advised in clinical use. Dietetic bodies caution about the carnivore end of the spectrum, citing low fibre and higher LDL cholesterol.
deepLead:
Ketovore is an informal label for a diet that combines ketogenic, very low-carbohydrate eating with a meat-heavy emphasis, while still allowing some plant foods. It sits between a standard ketogenic diet and the carnivore diet, which allows only animal products .
The ketogenic diet is a high-fat, adequate-protein, low-carbohydrate diet used in conventional medicine mainly for drug-resistant epilepsy . The carnivore diet is classed by dietetic bodies such as the British Dietetic Association as a fad diet, and no clinical trials of it were cited on Wikipedia . No clinical trials of a diet specifically called ketovore were found.

name: Eat like a bodybuilder (rice/chicken/broccoli)

angle.text: Users adopt the rice, chicken and broccoli template to gain muscle or cut fat with very few food decisions, building a leaner, more muscular physique. The underlying principles of protein intake and calorie control are well studied; the specific three-food menu is a convention rather than a tested protocol.

summary: The classic bro diet: lean protein, rice and greens, built on calorie control rather than any special food.
note: Repetitive menus can be hard to sustain; the pattern itself has no dedicated trials.
currentQuick:
This is the traditional bodybuilding menu of chicken, rice and broccoli, eaten in planned portions across bulking and cutting phases.
No trial has tested this exact meal set, but its principles of calorie surplus or deficit and high protein are widely discussed in sports nutrition.
How it works: A calorie surplus with adequate protein supports muscle gain alongside training, and a deficit supports fat loss. Simple repeated foods make intake easy to measure.
Risks and caveats: Risks depend on the amounts and on any extreme contest-prep methods such as dehydration. Very repetitive menus may limit variety, and individual needs differ.
deepLead:
Eating like a bodybuilder, often shorthand for plain rice, chicken breast and broccoli, is a long-standing fitness diet built around high protein, measured carbohydrate and low added fat. It is used in appearance communities to gain muscle or lose fat while keeping food choices simple.
Wikipedia describes competitive bodybuilders alternating between bulking, a calorie surplus to build muscle, and cutting, a deficit begun about 12 to 14 weeks before a contest . Typical foods include chicken, turkey, beef, fish, eggs, dairy and slow-digesting carbohydrates .
No clinical trial has tested the specific rice, chicken and broccoli meal pattern as such; the underlying principles of calorie balance and protein intake are discussed in sports nutrition.

name: Meal prep

chain: Steady fat loss or muscle gain
angle.text: Meal prep is used to hit calorie and protein targets consistently, which supports fat loss or muscle gain and a better physique over time. Small studies link it to better eating habits; its direct effect on appearance has not been measured.

summary: Cook ahead, portion it out; a habit tool for hitting diet targets, with small studies linking it to better habits.
note: Food-safety storage matters for pre-cooked meals.
currentQuick:
Meal prep means cooking and portioning meals in advance, usually weekly. Fitness communities use it to keep calories and protein on target.
Studies are small. One six-week program reported better cooking habits and body composition.
How it works: Having portioned meals ready reduces decision-making and unplanned eating, which supporters say makes a diet easier to follow.
Risks and caveats: Stored cooked food can grow bacteria if kept or reheated improperly, and some plastic containers can shed microplastics when heated.
deepLead:
Meal prep is the practice of planning and cooking meals in advance, often a week at a time, and storing them in portioned containers . In fitness and appearance communities it is used to control calories and protein and to avoid unplanned eating.
Wikipedia notes people use it to lose weight, build muscle or keep a healthy lifestyle, and links frequent home cooking with lower type 2 diabetes risk . A small published program study reported that a six-week group-based advanced meal prep course improved cooking attitudes, behaviours and body composition .

name: Hot-sauce thermogenics / spicy food

angle.text: Forum posters eat chili and hot sauce, or take capsaicin supplements, hoping to speed metabolism and trim body fat for a leaner look. Capsaicin has been studied for appetite and energy expenditure, with small effects reported and weak evidence for visible weight loss.

summary: Spicy food as a metabolism booster; capsaicin may nudge appetite slightly, but weight-loss evidence is weak.
note: Capsaicin pills have been linked to rare serious cardiac events in case reports.
currentQuick:
Some dieters add hot sauce, chilies or capsaicin supplements hoping to raise metabolism and lose fat.
Reviews cited on Wikipedia found no direct link between capsaicin and weight loss, with weak evidence of a small effect on food intake.
How it works: Capsaicin activates the TRPV1 heat-and-pain receptor on sensory nerves. Proponents say this triggers extra heat production and reduced appetite.
Risks and caveats: Capsaicin can irritate the mouth, stomach, skin and eyes, causing nausea or diarrhea. Isolated case reports describe serious events from concentrated pills or extreme spicy challenges.
deepLead:
Hot-sauce thermogenics refers to eating chili peppers, hot sauce or capsaicin supplements in the belief that the heat speeds metabolism and helps fat loss. Capsaicin, the pungent compound in chilies, binds the TRPV1 receptor on pain-sensing nerves, producing sensations of heat .
Wikipedia reports that a 2007 source found no evidence linking capsaicin ingestion directly to weight loss, and a 2014 meta-analysis found weak evidence that capsaicin before a meal might slightly reduce intake . Large doses can irritate and cause nausea, vomiting and abdominal pain .

name: Sea moss / chlorella / spirulina

angle.text: Sea moss gels and chlorella or spirulina powders are promoted as superfoods for glowing skin and energy. The nutrient content of the algae is documented, while appearance effects have not been tested in trials and rest largely on marketing and anecdote.

summary: Algae powders and gels marketed as superfood skin-and-energy boosters, with no appearance trials behind them.
note: Contamination (microcystins, heavy metals) and iodine content are documented concerns.
currentQuick:
Sea moss (Irish moss), chlorella and spirulina are algae products sold as superfood supplements for general wellness, skin and energy.
Public health sources say evidence is insufficient to recommend them for any human condition, and no studies were found testing them for appearance.
How it works: They are nutrient-dense foods (protein, minerals, carrageenan in sea moss), and proponents attribute wider benefits to this content; published research has not established such effects.
Risks and caveats: Reported concerns include microcystin and heavy-metal contamination of some products, allergic reactions, drug interactions, high iodine in sea moss, and FDA warning letters over false health claims for chlorella products.
deepLead:
Sea moss, chlorella and spirulina are algae-based products sold as dietary supplements and 'superfoods'. Sea moss usually refers to Irish moss (Chondrus crispus), a red seaweed of North Atlantic coasts rich in the thickener carrageenan . Chlorella is a genus of single-celled green algae , and spirulina is the dried biomass of cyanobacteria, mainly of the genus Arthrospira .
They are promoted in wellness and appearance-oriented circles for general nutrition, skin, energy and 'detox'. Public health bodies have not endorsed these uses: the US National Institutes of Health has said the evidence is insufficient to recommend spirulina for any human condition , and the American Cancer Society has said available studies do not support chlorella for preventing or treating disease .

name: Greens powders (AG1)

chain: Claimed better nutrition and gut health
angle.text: Greens powders such as AG1 are taken as a daily all-in-one supplement, with users crediting them for better skin, digestion and energy. Brand-supported trials are small and focus on nutrient status; appearance effects have not been tested.

summary: A heavily podcast-marketed daily greens drink whose supporting trials are small and whose appearance effects are untested.
note: Some ingredient amounts sit inside proprietary blends; cost is about US$79 per month (2024).
currentQuick:
Greens powders are mixed-ingredient powders (vegetables, algae, vitamins, minerals) taken as a daily drink. AG1 is the leading brand and is sold by subscription, mostly via influencer and podcast promotion.
Critics quoted in coverage call its supporting trials very small. No studies were found on appearance outcomes.
How it works: The product supplies a broad mix of micronutrients and plant ingredients; claimed benefits are general-health ones, and critics argue each ingredient is present in small amounts.
Risks and caveats: No specific harms are described in the sources used here. Reported issues are cost and proprietary-blend labelling that withholds some ingredient amounts.
deepLead:
Greens powders are powdered blends of vegetables, algae, herbs, vitamins and minerals mixed into water as a daily supplement. The best-known brand is AG1, formerly Athletic Greens, a Nevada-based company founded in December 2010 by Chris Ashenden that sells a roughly 75-ingredient powder by subscription .
AG1 is marketed heavily through podcasts and influencers, with creators paid through affiliate arrangements . Critics quoted in coverage, including a Harvard Medical School professor, have described the supporting trials as very small, and have questioned the value of a many-ingredient blend .

name: Tapeworm / sanitized parasite diet

angle.text: The tapeworm diet is a fringe weight-loss idea in which people look to a parasite to reduce how many calories they absorb, aiming for a thinner body. It is untested as a weight-loss method and is not an accepted medical approach.

summary: Fringe idea of swallowing a parasite to lose weight; untested, and parasitic infection carries serious documented risks.
note: Neurocysticercosis from tapeworm infection can cause seizures and death.
currentQuick:
The tapeworm diet is a fringe notion of deliberately ingesting a tapeworm, or a pill said to contain one, to lose weight.
No studies were found testing it, and it is not an accepted medical treatment.
How it works: Proponents' idea is that a parasite absorbs part of the host's nutrient intake; no research was found supporting this as a weight-loss method.
Risks and caveats: Infection with Taenia solium can cause cysticercosis, including brain cysts and seizures, and in severe cases death; treatment also needs monitoring.
deepLead:
The tapeworm or 'sanitized parasite' diet refers to the idea of deliberately ingesting a tapeworm, or a product claimed to contain one, in order to lose weight. It is discussed as a fringe weight-loss method, not an accepted medical treatment.
Tapeworm infection is a recognised medical condition. For the pork tapeworm Taenia solium, swallowing eggs can cause cysticercosis, in which cysts can form in the brain; the resulting neurocysticercosis is described as the leading cause of seizures worldwide .

name: Chewing and spitting

angle.text: Chewing and spitting appears in appearance communities as a way to enjoy food while avoiding its calories for a leaner look. In clinical literature it is documented as a behaviour seen in eating disorders and a marker of severity, not as a studied appearance method.

summary: An eating-disorder behaviour studied in clinics as a marker of severity, not a researched appearance method.
note: Described in the literature as a compensatory behaviour associated with eating disorders; support is available through clinicians.
currentQuick:
Chewing and spitting means chewing food and spitting it out instead of swallowing. In research it is documented as a behaviour in people with eating disorders, such as bulimia.
Published studies are clinical descriptions of patients; none tests it as a way to improve appearance.
How it works: Studies describe it as a compensatory behaviour used to avoid calorie intake while experiencing taste, and it has been linked to binge eating.
Risks and caveats: Papers report it as a marker of greater psychopathology and behavioural severity in inpatients with eating disorders [6]. Anyone affected can seek help from a clinician or an eating-disorder helpline.
deepLead:
Chewing and spitting is a behaviour in which a person chews food for taste and then spits it out without swallowing. In clinical literature it is described as a compensatory or purging-type behaviour seen in people with eating disorders.
In a 1985 study of 275 patients meeting criteria for bulimia, 64.5 percent reported chewing and spitting out food, alongside binge eating (100 percent), self-induced vomiting (88.1 percent) and laxative use (60.6 percent) . Later studies have examined it as a marker of eating-disorder severity .

name: Extended fasting 'dopamine fasts'

chain: Weight loss and a leaner look
angle.text: Extended fasts are used for rapid weight loss, while dopamine fasts, which cut phone use, gaming and porn, are promoted for focus, discipline and a mental reset that supports habits like training and sleep. Food fasting is studied for weight loss; the behavioural version is loosely defined and untested for looks.

summary: Abstaining from food or stimulation to 'reset'; the behavioural version is loosely defined and extended fasting carries real medical risks.
note: Refeeding syndrome after prolonged fasting can be fatal.
currentQuick:
Two practices share this entry: multi-day food fasting, and dopamine fasting, where people avoid stimulating habits such as phones or gaming.
No studies were found on appearance outcomes, and experts quoted in coverage dispute the 'reset' framing of dopamine fasting.
How it works: Extended fasting shifts the body into ketosis. Dopamine fasting is described by its originator as reducing impulsive behaviour, not lowering dopamine itself.
Risks and caveats: Prolonged fasting can cause electrolyte loss, gallstones, lean-mass loss and refeeding syndrome, which can be fatal. Dopamine fasting has no specific physical harms reported, though critics call its premise unscientific.
deepLead:
This entry covers two separate practices: prolonged food fasting (going beyond 24 hours without eating, often 5 to 20 days) and 'dopamine fasting', in which a person abstains from stimulating behaviours such as phone use, gaming or pornography .
Dopamine fasting was developed as a cognitive behavioural approach by California psychologist Cameron Sepah and attracted media coverage in late 2019 . Sepah says the aim is to reduce impulsive behaviours, not literally to lower dopamine; some neuroscientists have criticised the idea that the brain can be 'reset' this way .

name: Alkaline water / alkaline diet

angle.text: Followers of the alkaline diet and alkaline water say they improve skin, energy and general health by shifting body pH. The diet's emphasis on fruit and vegetables is conventional, while the pH mechanism and any appearance benefit have not been shown in studies.

summary: Diet and water pH claims that dietitians and cancer charities say do not change blood pH; no appearance studies exist.
note: Restrictive versions can cause nutrient gaps; cost of ionizers and supplements.
currentQuick:
The alkaline diet and alkaline water rest on the idea that what you eat or drink shifts body pH and thereby health. The diet favours plants and excludes most animal foods and grains.
Reviews report no evidence that diet changes blood pH in healthy people, and no appearance studies were found.
How it works: Proponents say foods leave acidic or alkaline residues that affect the body; physiologists note blood pH is tightly regulated, and urine pH does not reflect body acidity.
Risks and caveats: Excluding food groups can cause nutrient deficiencies, and cancer organisations caution against relying on it; promoters often sell supplements and equipment.
deepLead:
The alkaline diet is a group of loosely related diets based on the idea that foods change the body's pH and that this affects disease. It favours most fruit and vegetables and excludes most grains, meat, cheese and eggs. Alkaline water, often made with ionizer machines, is marketed on a similar premise .
Proponents have promoted these for energy, weight loss and disease prevention. Reviews and professional bodies report that diet does not meaningfully change blood pH in healthy people, which is tightly regulated between 7.35 and 7.45 .

name: Detox teas / juice cleanses

angle.text: Users take detox teas and juice cleanses for clearer skin, a leaner face and reduced bloating. Short-term scale and bloat changes are commonly reported; the claim of removing toxins is not supported by reviews, and skin effects are untested.

summary: Teas and cleanses sold to flush out 'toxins'; reviews find no good evidence they do.
note: Prolonged fasting and some cleanses have documented harms.
currentQuick:
Detox teas and juice cleanses are marketed as ways to purge toxins, with promised benefits such as clearer skin and a leaner look.
Published reviews have found no compelling evidence that detox diets remove toxins or help with weight beyond short-term loss that is regained.
How it works: Proponents say cleansing helps the body release accumulated contaminants. Clinicians note that the liver and kidneys already process most ingested toxins.
Risks and caveats: Prolonged fasting can be dangerous, and a kidney injury case was linked to a green-smoothie cleanse. Belief in detox can also delay medical care.
deepLead:
Detox teas and juice cleanses are consumer products and short-term diets marketed as ways to remove unspecified "toxins" from the body. They are part of the wider alternative-medicine category of detoxification, which also includes fasting, colon cleansing and restricted diets . In appearance-focused communities they are discussed mainly in connection with clearer skin, a leaner face and reduced bloating.
Proponents say that modern food and the environment leave contaminants that accumulate in the body and that a cleanse helps release them . Published reviews have found no compelling evidence that detox diets remove toxins or aid weight management, and a 2015 critical review in the Journal of Human Nutrition and Dietetics called for independent regulatory review of such products .

name: Fruit juice cleanse

angle.text: Juice cleanses are done over a few days as a reset, with people hoping for glowing skin, less bloat and quick weight loss. Short-term weight change is expected from reduced calories, while the detox and skin claims have no published research behind them.

summary: A days-long juice-only diet sold as a reset; no published research backs the detox or skin claims.
note: Risks include dehydration and metabolic problems in people with diabetes.
currentQuick:
A juice cleanse means drinking only fruit and vegetable juice for a few days, usually to detox or reset. It is popular online and among celebrities.
Health bodies such as the American Cancer Society and Harvard Health state there is no scientific evidence for the claimed benefits.
How it works: Believers say it clears toxins; dietitians say the liver and kidneys already do that work. Weight lost is mostly regained afterwards according to reviews.
Risks and caveats: Possible dizziness, dehydration, electrolyte disturbance and metabolic crises in people with undiagnosed diabetes; long unsupervised fasts can cause deficiencies.
deepLead:
A fruit juice cleanse, also called juice fasting or juice cleansing, is a short-term diet, usually one to seven days, in which a person drinks only fruit and vegetable juices and eats no solid food . It is promoted as a way to detoxify the body and is treated as a form of detox diet .
Proponents say periodic cleanses remove unwanted chemicals . Organisations including the American Cancer Society and Harvard Health state that there is no scientific evidence supporting juice-only diets for such benefits .

name: Cold-pressed oils / olive oil

chain: Swap seed oils for olive oil
Different fatty acid and polyphenol intake
angle.text: Looksmaxxers promote extra virgin olive oil and other cold-pressed oils as a replacement for refined seed oils, citing skin and general health. Olive oil has regulator-qualified heart-health claims; its effect on appearance has not been tested.

summary: Mechanically extracted oils, chiefly olive, promoted as a seed-oil swap; heart-health claims are regulator-qualified, appearance effects untested.
note: Labelling and adulteration issues exist in the olive oil market.
currentQuick:
Cold-pressed oils, especially extra virgin olive oil, are made without heat or solvents and are promoted as alternatives to refined seed oils.
Regulators allow limited health claims about heart disease when olive oil replaces saturated fat; effects on appearance have not been established in the sources reviewed.
How it works: The oil is rich in oleic acid and polyphenols, which are sensitive to heat, light and oxygen.
Risks and caveats: Few direct risks are reported; documented concerns involve fraud and mislabelling, and the FDA claim is described as limited and not conclusive.
deepLead:
Cold-pressed oils, most prominently extra virgin olive oil, are edible oils extracted mechanically without heat or chemical solvents. In looksmaxxing and wider diet-culture discussion they are promoted as replacements for refined seed oils, with claims about skin and general health .
Extra virgin olive oil is the top grade under International Olive Council standards, requiring cold mechanical extraction and free acidity of no more than 0.8 percent . In the US the FDA allows a qualified health claim that limited and not conclusive evidence suggests about two tablespoons daily may reduce coronary heart disease risk when replacing saturated fat .

name: Butter / ghee

chain: Dairy fats instead of seed oils
angle.text: Butter and ghee are promoted in ancestral and looksmaxxing diet circles as alternatives to vegetable oils, linked to skin health and hormone support. Appearance effects have not been studied; guidelines address them mainly through saturated fat.

summary: Dairy fats promoted over vegetable oils; guidelines advise limiting them for saturated fat, appearance effects untested.
note: Health bodies advise limiting saturated fat.
currentQuick:
Butter and ghee are dairy fats that some communities favour over vegetable oils.
Health bodies advise limiting them for saturated fat, while a 2016 meta-analysis found small or insignificant associations with mortality at modest intake.
How it works: They are mostly saturated and monounsaturated fat with vitamin A; ghee has milk solids removed and a higher smoke point.
Risks and caveats: Higher LDL cholesterol with replacement of plant oils; ghee on newborn umbilical wounds was linked to neonatal tetanus.
deepLead:
Butter is a dairy fat made by churning cream, about 80 percent butterfat, and ghee is a South Asian clarified butter simmered until its milk solids are removed . In looksmaxxing and ancestral-diet communities they are promoted as alternatives to vegetable oils.
Health authorities cited in reference works advise limiting both because of saturated fat: the UK NHS advises eating butter less often, and the WHO's 2023 guidance is cited as recommending plant oils over ghee . A 2016 meta-analysis found small or insignificant associations between about 14 grams of butter a day and mortality or cardiovascular disease .

name: Grass-fed beef / ethical-sourcing

angle.text: Grass-fed beef is favoured for protein, omega-3 and CLA content and for ethical sourcing, as part of eating for muscle and skin. Fatty acid differences from grain-fed beef are measured; appearance benefits specific to grass-fed beef are unstudied.

summary: Pasture-raised beef touted for more omega-3 and CLA; differences exist but appearance benefits are unstudied.
currentQuick:
Grass-fed beef is meat from cattle raised mainly on forage. Advocates cite nutrient and ethical advantages.
Studies report leaner meat with somewhat more omega-3 and CLA, but health and environmental conclusions are often inconclusive.
How it works: Diet changes the fat profile of the meat; no mechanism for facial appearance effects has been tested.
Risks and caveats: No distinct risks are reported; the sources note mixed findings on pathogens and that labelling is inconsistently regulated.
deepLead:
Grass-fed beef comes from cattle reared mainly on forage rather than grain-based finishing feed. It is promoted in diet and looksmaxxing circles for nutrient density and ethical sourcing .
Reference material reports that grass-fed meat tends to be leaner and to contain more conjugated linoleic acid and omega-3 fatty acids than grain-fed meat . Many health and environmental conclusions on the topic are described as inconclusive .

name: Sardines / oily fish

angle.text: Sardines and other oily fish are eaten as a cheap source of omega-3 fats, B12 and protein, with users linking them to better skin. Omega-3 intake is widely studied for health; skin benefits from eating oily fish were not tested in the sources reviewed.

summary: Cheap oily fish with B12 and omega-3; skin benefits are claimed but untested in the sources reviewed.
note: Pacific sardine fisheries have faced closures.
currentQuick:
Sardines are small oily fish eaten for protein, omega-3 and micronutrients. Some in appearance communities promote them for skin.
No clinical studies on sardines for skin were found in the sources reviewed.
How it works: The claimed route is omega-3 intake; the nutrition data note high B12 and calcium but give no omega-3 figure.
Risks and caveats: Sardines are described as lower in mercury than many fish; canned versions contain notable sodium.
deepLead:
Sardines are small, oily forage fish eaten fresh, grilled, smoked or canned. In appearance-focused diet discussion they are promoted as a source of omega-3 fatty acids said to benefit skin .
Canned Pacific sardines are notable for protein and vitamin B12, with 375 percent of the daily value per 100 grams, and provide calcium when eaten with bones . The reference article gives no omega-3 quantities and cites no clinical studies on skin .

name: Eggs (egg yolk)

angle.text: Eggs and yolks are a staple of bodybuilding and appearance diets as a cheap, complete protein with fat and choline, supporting muscle gain. Egg protein quality is well documented; the appearance effect comes through overall protein and calorie intake.

summary: A staple protein-and-choline food; its appearance relevance is mostly indirect.
currentQuick:
Eggs are an everyday food that provide protein, fat and choline. They appear in muscle-building and general diet discussions.
No published trials were found testing egg yolk specifically for skin, hair or other appearance outcomes.
How it works: Eggs supply complete protein and nutrients such as choline and B vitamins as part of the overall diet.
Risks and caveats: Research on dietary cholesterol is mixed; several meta-analyses found no link to heart disease at moderate intake. Raw eggs can carry salmonella, and egg allergy is common in infants.
deepLead:
Whole eggs and egg yolks are a common food in bodybuilding and general nutrition, and are discussed in appearance-focused communities mainly as sources of protein, fat and choline. A hard-boiled chicken egg provides roughly 12.6 g of protein and 294 mg of choline per 100 g, and egg protein scores the maximum on the PDCAAS protein-quality scale.
Debate about eggs has centred on dietary cholesterol (about 373 mg per 100 g). Meta-analyses published in the 2010s and 2020s reached differing conclusions, with several finding no association between moderate egg intake and cardiovascular risk in the general population. Wikipedia notes that raw eggs carry a salmonella risk and that cooked egg protein is more bioavailable than raw.

name: Oats / rice-and-chicken carbs for bulking

angle.text: Lifters build a bulk around oats, rice and chicken to eat in a calorie surplus affordably and add muscle for a bigger physique. The link between positive energy balance and muscle growth is well established; the specific foods are a convention.

summary: The cheap carb-and-chicken staple diet for a calorie-surplus bulk.
note: Larger surpluses add more body fat.
currentQuick:
This is the common bulking pattern of eating oats, rice and chicken in a calorie surplus to gain muscle.
The general principle of surplus eating for hypertrophy is widely accepted; the specific foods have not been trialled as a set.
How it works: A positive energy balance combined with adequate protein supports muscle growth alongside resistance training.
Risks and caveats: Larger surpluses and longer bulks add more body fat, and some lifters report needing a harder cut afterward.
deepLead:
A "standard bulk" built around oats, rice and chicken refers to eating in a calorie surplus using inexpensive carbohydrate and lean-protein staples in order to gain muscle. Bulking in general means eating above maintenance energy needs, and Wikipedia reports a well-established link between positive energy balance and muscle growth.
Bodybuilding references describe preferences for slower-digesting carbohydrates, and note that a larger surplus or longer bulk adds more body fat. The specific foods oats, rice and chicken are not singled out in the sources reviewed.

name: Sweet potato / carb timing

chain: Better training and recovery, more muscle
angle.text: Lifters schedule carbs such as sweet potato around training to fuel sessions and speed recovery, in pursuit of more muscle. Glycogen replacement after exercise is studied, while the benefit of exact timing for physique is debated.

summary: Scheduling carbs like sweet potato around workouts; the timing effect itself is debated.
currentQuick:
Carb timing is the practice of eating carbohydrates such as sweet potato at set times around training.
The "anabolic window" idea is presented as a suggestion rather than established, and sweet potato has not been studied specifically.
How it works: Carbohydrates replenish muscle glycogen used in high-intensity exercise, which proponents say speeds recovery.
Risks and caveats: No specific risks are documented for this practice beyond general dietary considerations.
deepLead:
Carbohydrate timing refers to the idea that when carbohydrates are eaten around training affects performance and recovery. Wikipedia describes nutrient timing as coordinating intake with exercise, with claims that carbohydrates during and after workouts help replace muscle glycogen.
A suggested post-exercise "anabolic window" of about 15 to 45 minutes is described as a suggestion rather than an established fact, and the article says timing is not essential to good performance. Sweet potato as a particular carbohydrate source was not covered by the sources reviewed.

name: Eating disorder-adjacent restriction ('thinspo' leanness)

angle.text: Some appearance communities discuss extreme restriction to reach a gaunt or very lean look, often through thinspo content. Medical groups treat this pattern as eating disorder risk, and it is described in clinical literature rather than studied as an appearance method.

summary: Extreme restriction for a gaunt look, closely tied to eating disorder content.
note: Associated with documented eating disorder harms; seek professional support if affected.
currentQuick:
This entry covers restrictive eating aimed at extreme leanness, sharing ground with thinspiration and pro-ana content.
Medical organisations criticise such content, and research links exposure to worse mood and body image.
How it works: It involves severe caloric restriction and appearance-comparison content; no instructional detail is given here.
Risks and caveats: Anorexia nervosa is reported to have among the highest mortality of psychiatric disorders.[1] Support is available through eating disorder helplines and clinicians.
deepLead:
Thinspiration ("thinspo") is imagery and content of thin people, associated with pro-ana (pro-anorexia) online communities that promote behaviours linked to anorexia nervosa. In looksmaxxing contexts, extreme restriction to reach a lean or gaunt look is sometimes discussed, and medical groups regard restrictive eating of this kind as carrying eating disorder risk.
Eating disorder organisations such as ANAD, NEDA and the Academy for Eating Disorders have criticised pro-ana sites for glamorising illness. If you or someone you know is affected, local eating disorder helplines and healthcare providers offer support.
